name: Felix Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do parcels for one of the apps, out of the depot by the bypass, and I cover the villages south of town in my own estate car. Most days it's fifty to seventy drops, back roads, farm tracks, a lot of dogs. Fridays and Saturdays I do takeaway in town for a few hours because it pays well. I've been doing it nine months and I still get the odd village wrong, but I like the quiet and the same faces.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you do before, and how's the money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was on the shop floor at a DIY store for four years, stacking and helping customers. I lived with my mum until last year and saved most of it, so I've got about ten months put away. My girlfriend Hanna is a hairdresser and we split the rent on a small flat. The delivery pays better than the shop did, as long as I do the weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Every couple of years there's some big thing that's going to change everything, and it doesn't. I wouldn't post anything; I'm not really an online person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I can carry on, which is what I want. I've found something that pays and that I'm getting the hang of. I don't need it to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now: parcels in the week, takeaway at the weekend, put money away. Maybe service the car before winter and get new tyres. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really, because I've only just got the hang of this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any of the AI tools people talk about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, never. The app tells me where to go and that's enough technology for me. Hanna uses something on her phone to write the salon's posts, but I don't touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the job that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting a ticket for parking on a narrow lane, and the car breaking down, because it's my car and my problem. The app doesn't pay for repairs. Other than that it's a decent job.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because big changes rarely arrive.
I **wouldn't post** anything, because I'm not an online person.
think: It means I can **carry on**, which is what I want.
I've found something that **pays better** than the shop and I'm getting the hang of it.
do: Keep **parcels in the week** and takeaway at the weekend.
**Service the car** and fit new tyres before winter.
S0.quote: The app tells me where to go and that's enough technology for me.
fieldNote: Wants **no change**; he has just found a routine that works.
Has **ten months saved**, so this picture feels secure.
His only worries are **car costs** and parking tickets.
Never uses AI and sees **no reason** to start.

steps.text: Keep the village parcel round and weekend takeaway shifts
Put part of each week's pay into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to keep an eye on it but not to panic. Some jobs change, some don't. I'd probably say that to Gary at the depot over a coffee and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think my job's fine for a good while. No machine is finding a back gate down a farm track any time soon. Mrs Holt's gate took me three goes. But I'd worry about the app changing things I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd keep going and see. Maybe keep a bit more in savings than usual. If the app brought in some new AI feature, I'd use the simplest version and ignore the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like hearing a noise from the engine you can't place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says thinking tasks go first and robots come more slowly. Which part of your day is thinking work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The app does the route and the customer messages already. My bit is driving, finding the place and handing it over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk it over with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hanna, and maybe my mum. Hanna's better with this stuff and would tell me what's real. My mum would tell me to keep my head down and work.

I'd tell Gary at the depot that **some jobs change** and some don't.
think: My job is **fine for a while**, because farm tracks are hard to automate.
I worry about the **app changing** things I don't understand.
do: Keep a bit **more in savings** than usual.
Use only the **simplest version** of any new app feature.
feel: **Uneasy**, like an engine noise he can't place yet.
S1.quote: No machine is finding a back gate down a farm track any time soon.
fieldNote: He correctly sees his day as **mostly hands-on**.
Main fear is not robots but **changes he can't follow**.
Leans on **Hanna** to tell him what's real.
Pragmatic and **calm in tone**, but not fully at ease.

steps.text: Keep doing the same parcel round in the southern villages
Wait and see what the app changes before doing anything
Keep a bit more in savings than the usual monthly amount

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's out of our hands, so there's no point shouting about it. Somebody would say it's the end of the world, and I'd say let's see. I'd keep quiet online, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd lose this by 2031, maybe a bit later out in the villages. And I don't have anything else; I'm not a trades person. That would keep me up, thinking about it at three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything extra; Hanna and I were going to go away next summer, and that would wait. I'd keep driving as long as there was work. I'd look at going back to the DIY store or a warehouse, something with a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in the stomach, honestly. Like I just got settled and the ground went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots doing hands-on work by 2031. What does that mean for the village round?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The villages might last a year or two longer than town, because of the tracks and the dogs. But a year or two isn't a career. Probably I'd be one of the last drivers out there, on worse pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep it, and not touch it. Ten months of savings sounds a lot until you've got no job. I'd only spend it if I really had to.

say: I'd say it's **out of our hands**, so shouting won't help.
I'd say **let's see** when people call it the end of the world.
think: I'd **lose this job** by 2031, maybe a bit later in the villages.
I have **no trade** to fall back on, and that would keep me up.
do: Put off the **summer holiday** with Hanna and stop extra spending.
Keep **driving** as long as there's work.
Look at going back to **DIY or a warehouse** job with a contract.
feel: **Sick in the stomach**, like the ground went just as he got settled.
S2.quote: Ten months of savings sounds a lot until you've got no job.
fieldNote: Says it's out of our hands in public but is **losing sleep** privately.
Expects to **lose the job** within five years with no trade.
His fallback is **familiar work**, the DIY store or a warehouse.
**Savings** are a shield he won't touch unless forced.

steps.text: Postpone next summer's holiday with Hanna
Keep driving the village round while parcels are still there
Ask the DIY store about a contracted stockroom job
Leave the ten months of savings untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so no need to panic yet. People would argue about it online and I'd stay out of it. I'd just say keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time, but I've got no idea what to use it for. I'd probably keep driving and hope something turns up. That's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep driving, keep saving. Maybe after a couple of years ask around about warehouse jobs or the DIY store again. I'd wait and see what other drivers do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not sick. More like a bill I know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'm not doing it all at once. I'd have time to see if the robots actually work in the villages. With two years I'd be grabbing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not a trades person. Would you try one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Gary keeps talking about forklift licences. If he did it and it worked out, I might do it too. I'm not going to be first.

say: I'd say there are **a few years**, so no need to panic yet.
I'd **stay out** of arguments online and just say keep working.
think: I'd have **time** but no idea what to use it for.
I'd probably **keep driving** and hope something turns up.
do: Keep **driving and saving** for the next couple of years.

Wait and see what **other drivers** do before choosing.
feel: **Anxious**, but not sick, like a bill he knows is coming.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time, but I've got no idea what to use it for.
fieldNote: The extra time **eases panic** but doesn't create a plan.
He'd follow **Gary** into a forklift licence rather than lead.

Still expects his **income to go**, so anxious.

steps.text: Keep driving the village parcel round for two more years
Keep putting money into savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and loads can change. I'd probably say it's a problem for later. I'd not post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it feels far off. I'd be thirty-nine, and maybe settled with Hanna and a mortgage. It'd still bother me, but not now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much this year. Keep driving, keep saving, maybe look at a forklift licence in a few years. I'd start properly worrying around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not much more than that, because 2039 feels like somebody else's problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots around 2039. How old will you be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirty-nine. By then I'd want something with a contract and a pension anyway. So maybe it pushes me where I should be going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd do the same as now, and I know that's probably not the clever answer, but it's the honest one.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long time** and loads can change.
I'd call it **a problem for later** and keep quiet online.
think: It feels **far off**; I'd be thirty-nine and maybe settled.
It would **bother me** eventually, but not now.
do: Keep **driving and saving** with no changes this year.
Look at a **forklift licence** in a few years.
S4.quote: I'd do the same as now, and I know that's probably not the clever answer, but it's the honest one.
fieldNote: A decade lets him **put it off**, which suits his resistance.
Sees a contracted job with a **pension** as a natural next step anyway.
Honest that he'd **change nothing** this year.
His **savings and age** keep the worry low.

steps.text: Keep the parcel round and weekend takeaway shifts unchanged
Keep saving monthly towards a future flat deposit
Wait until about 2034 before looking at a forklift licence

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have three years before the robots, and no trade and no plan. What would help is someone showing me which jobs nearby would still need people, and a paid course for something like forklifts or warehouse work, so I don't have to guess.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how people like me find out about this stuff. I don't read the news much. If robots are coming, somebody should tell drivers properly, because nobody at the depot talks about it.

headlineQuote: If robots are coming, somebody should tell drivers properly, because nobody at the depot talks about it.
portrait: Felix is a **27-year-old** parcel driver covering the villages south of town in his own car.
He has **ten months saved** and lives with Hanna, a hairdresser.
He prefers **routine**, never uses AI and would follow others rather than lead.
He's **pragmatic**, blames no one and calls it out of our hands.
He's calm in slow pictures but **alarmed** when robots arrive by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd face robots with no trade and no plan.
whatWouldHelp: Clear information on **which local jobs** would still need people.
A **paid course** for forklift or warehouse work.
